models.model_selection_guide:
Claude Opus 5: I would use Opus for difficult regulatory questions, deeper reasoning, and work where I need to compare sources carefully.

Claude Sonnet 5: I would use Sonnet for most of my normal coursework, coding, research, and technical writing.

Claude Haiku 4.5: I would use Haiku for quick tasks such as formatting, extraction, simple file changes, and other mechanical work.

reasoning_chain_test.prompt: See session log entry: Reasoning Chain Test
reasoning_chain_test.observation: Claude did not force the answer into RG 5.71 or 10 CFR 73.54 just because the prompt named those documents. It identified 10 CFR 73.77 as the actual reporting rule and correctly focused on the difference between the one-hour and four-hour reporting categories and the fact that the clock starts after discovery. The reasoning also helped expose uncertainty around what counts as an adverse impact and when discovery actually happens. One issue I found was that it discussed the older 2010 version of RG 5.71, while the current revision is Rev. 1 from 2023, so the source version still needed manual verification. I later confirmed this: RG 5.71 Rev. 1 was issued February 2023 under ADAMS ML22258A204 and published at 88 FR 9117. In a later session Claude went further and reported that the Rev. 1 accession number could not be verified and was possibly fabricated, which was wrong. My original catch was correct and Claude's correction to it was not. Rev. 1 also matters substantively here: it references 10 CFR 73.77 directly in Section C.3.3.2.6, which Rev. 0 could not, since 73.77 postdates it by five years.
reasoning_chain_test.nuclear_relevance: Regulatory work requires the model to identify the correct rule, use the current revision, and separate what the regulation actually says from what it is inferring. A confident answer based on an old document or the wrong reporting provision could lead to a wrong compliance decision, so I would still verify important regulatory conclusions against the NRC source.

vision_test.observation: Claude correctly identified the 11 systems, the Purdue levels, the separation boundary, and the main OT-SIEM connections. It correctly identified RMS to OT-SIEM, PSI to OT-SIEM, PPC to OT-SIEM, and OT-SIEM to ICT-SIEM. It also correctly noticed the one-way export and the RPS data diode. The main error was tracing the Access Interlocks line as PPC to DCS when the diagram shows it coming from PSI toward DCS. It also inferred some protocols that were not written on the image, so those should be treated as inference rather than fact.
vision_test.nuclear_relevance: I would trust the vision model to help identify system names, Purdue levels, labels, and obvious connections, but I would manually verify connection paths, arrow direction, crossing lines, and any inferred protocol. A wrong connection in a nuclear plant architecture could change the attack path and lead to a wrong security conclusion.

justification: Claude Code is useful for this course for three reasons. First, the reasoning test showed that Opus can challenge the wording of a question and identify a more relevant regulation instead of only following the documents named in the prompt. Second, the vision test showed that it can read a complex plant architecture diagram and identify most systems, levels, and OT-SIEM connections. Third, Claude Code works directly with the Markdown and JSON files used in this course, which makes it useful for drafting, reviewing, formatting, and updating workshop files while keeping the work in the repository.
limitations: The first limitation is source reliability, and it runs in both directions. During the reasoning test, Claude referred to the older 2010 version of RG 5.71 even though the current revision is Rev. 1 from 2023. In a later verification session it then incorrectly flagged the correct Rev. 1 accession number as unverifiable and downgraded three of my findings on that basis, so the tool both missed a current source and then wrongly rejected it. Regulatory sources need manual verification whether Claude is citing them or doubting them. The second limitation is diagram tracing. During the vision test, Claude incorrectly associated the Access Interlocks connection with PPC to DCS instead of PSI to DCS. It also inferred protocols that were not directly shown in the image. The third limitation is architecture grounding: Claude populated my attack surface maps with generic SIEM interfaces from NIST SP 800-82r3 Appendix E and did not include the connections the CS 581 plant architecture actually shows, so I had to add the RMS, PSI, and PPC feeds myself and mark the generic rows as unconfirmed. These tests showed that Claude can support the analysis, but I should not treat its regulatory claims, architecture connections, or its own self-corrections as verified facts without checking the original source.
